possible_confounders: Recent caffeine, alcohol, or nicotine use
control_variables: Time of day / hours since wake
boring_rival_explanations: Sensor noise floor differences across device units or placements unrelated to ANS
Stressor intensity variation across subjects (some subjects received weaker stressors)
Classifier decision threshold miscalibrated for population-level feature distributions
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If sensor noise floor is the primary driver, uncertainty will correlate with device-specific noise metrics (e.g., PPG SQI at rest) independent of ANS reactivity measures; subjects with matched ANS reactivity but different sensor noise floors will show divergent uncertainty.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: In a subsample with matched resting RMSSD and phasic EDA reactivity but different wearable device models (or placements) yielding different noise floors, stress-detection uncertainty tracks the sensor noise floor, not the ANS measures.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Must measure sensor noise floor per subject per session; consider multi-sensor fusion to isolate ANS vs. sensor contributions.

possible_confounders: Socioeconomic status (correlates with both skin phenotype and stress exposure)
control_variables: Ambient light (controlled lab or wearable light sensor)
Strap tension (pressure sensor or standardized protocol)
boring_rival_explanations: Demographic confounding: SES correlates with skin phenotype and chronic stress exposure, driving uncertainty via stressor differences not sensor physics
Differential stressor type/intensity across demographic groups
Algorithmic bias from training data imbalance across skin phenotypes
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If demographic confounding drives uncertainty, uncertainty will correlate with SES variables even after statistically controlling for melanin index and stratum corneum thickness; the skin phenotype effect will attenuate to non-significance when SES is included.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: In a sample matched on skin phenotype quartiles but varying in SES, uncertainty does not vary with SES; conversely, in a sample matched on SES but diverse in skin phenotype, uncertainty still varies with melanin index and stratum corneum thickness.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Require diverse recruitment across skin phenotype × SES cells; use multi-wavelength PPG to isolate melanin attenuation from perfusion changes.

possible_confounders: Shift work history or recent transmeridian travel
control_variables: Exclusion of shift workers and recent travelers
boring_rival_explanations: Time-of-day sensor drift (temperature-dependent PPG/EDA baseline shifts)
Diurnal variation in stressor type/intensity (e.g., work stress morning, social stress evening)
Fatigue effects on physiology unrelated to circadian phase
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If sensor drift causes uncertainty, uncertainty will correlate with device temperature or uptime, not with circadian phase × chronotype interaction; controlling for device temperature will eliminate the time-of-day effect.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: In a temperature-controlled lab environment (constant ambient and device temperature), the circadian phase × chronotype interaction on uncertainty persists, while device temperature shows no correlation with uncertainty.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Direct circadian phase measurement (DLMO) essential; consider adding time-of-day as explicit classifier feature to test if interaction disappears.

control_variables: GAD-7, PHQ-9, TAS-20 scores as covariates
MAIA score as covariate or stratification variable
boring_rival_explanations: High regulators have inherently more variable peripheral physiology (trait variability)
Regulation strategy correlates with interoceptive awareness, which affects self-report accuracy not physiology
Classifier feature set lacks regulation-specific physiological markers (e.g., facial EMG for suppression)
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If high regulators have inherently more variable physiology, their feature variability (within-subject variance) will be elevated during non-stress baseline periods as well as stress periods, not selectively during stress.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: During non-stress baseline epochs, high suppressors show comparable HRV/EDA within-subject variance to low suppressors; uncertainty elevation only appears during stress epochs where regulation is engaged.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Need state regulation assessment during each stressor; consider multi-modal features (cardiac, EDA, respiration) to capture regulation-specific signatures.

possible_confounders: Device charging routine (e.g., nightly vs. opportunistic)
Skin irritation or allergy to device materials
Occupational constraints (e.g., mandatory removal at work)
Battery life degradation over study period
control_variables: Job type and workplace wearable policy
boring_rival_explanations: Non-wear is random but high-stress subjects have more missing data by chance (sampling variability)
Non-wear correlates with high physical activity, not stress per se
Imputation method (mean, LOCF) introduces systematic bias unrelated to missingness mechanism
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If non-wear is random with respect to stress, the distribution of observed stress levels during wear periods will not differ between high and low non-wear subjects; retrospective stress recall during non-wear will show no association with non-wear timing.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: Subjects with high stress-correlated non-wear show similar observed stress levels during wear as low non-wear subjects, but retrospective EMA reveals significantly higher stress during non-wear epochs; pattern-mixture models confirm informative missingness.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Requires retrospective stress recall for non-wear periods; use accelerometer to distinguish non-wear from sedentary wear.

control_variables: VO2max or resting respiratory rate as fitness proxy
Speech detection from audio or accelerometer
boring_rival_explanations: HRV features are inherently noisy for all subjects regardless of RSA coupling
Classifier uses suboptimal HRV metrics (e.g., time-domain only) that are insensitive to vagal withdrawal
Stressor does not elicit consistent vagal withdrawal across subjects
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If HRV features are generally noisy, uncertainty will be uniformly high across all subjects regardless of RSA coupling strength; the correlation between RSA coupling and uncertainty will be near zero.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: Subjects with strong RSA coupling (high HF-HRV per unit respiratory depth) show low classifier uncertainty (tight predictive intervals, low entropy) during stress, while weak couplers show high uncertainty, despite identical stressor, sensor, and classifier.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Must measure respiration concurrently (thoracic impedance or accelerometry); paced breathing protocol to quantify coupling; test respiration-augmented classifier.

control_variables: Wrist circumference (tape measure) and bone prominence (ultrasound)
Fixed device model and strap across study
boring_rival_explanations: Signal quality differences due to device manufacturing variance across units
Algorithmic sensitivity to motion artifact varies by subject movement patterns
Skin perfusion physiology varies independently of placement tightness
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If manufacturing variance drives uncertainty, the same subject wearing different units of the same model at identical tightness will show different uncertainty levels; uncertainty will track device unit, not tightness.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: Same subject, same tightness (measured via strap tension sensor), different device units: uncertainty varies significantly across units. Same device unit, varying tightness: uncertainty follows U-shaped curve with minimum at optimal tightness.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Need objective tightness measurement (strap tension sensor); test multiple device units per subject; consider dynamic tightness changes during activity.

boring_rival_explanations: High allostatic load subjects have more comorbidities affecting sensor contact (edema, skin changes)
They experience qualitatively different stressors (chronic vs. acute) not captured by classifier
Classifier trained on healthier population lacks representation of high-load physiology
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If comorbidities affect sensor contact, signal quality metrics (PPG SQI, EDA impedance) will correlate with allostatic load index; controlling for signal quality will eliminate the allostatic load–uncertainty association.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: Signal quality metrics (PPG SQI, EDA impedance) show no correlation with allostatic load index, but feature dynamic range (stress vs. baseline HRV/EDA change) and class separation (Mahalanobis distance) still decline monotonically with allostatic load.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Allostatic load composite requires ≥6 biomarkers; longitudinal design needed for causal inference; test if personalized baselines reduce uncertainty.

possible_confounders: EMA prompt timing relative to stressor onset
Prompt content (stress vs. neutral vs. positive)
Reactivity to wearable device itself (novelty effect)
control_variables: Randomized prompt timing relative to stressors
Habituation period (≥7 days) before data collection
Heartbeat counting task accuracy as interoceptive accuracy measure
boring_rival_explanations: High interoceptive awareness improves self-report accuracy (labels more valid), not contaminates them
EMA reactivity is uniform across subjects but awareness affects baseline physiology
High awareness subjects have more stable physiology, making classification easier
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If awareness improves label accuracy, high awareness subjects will show better calibration (lower expected calibration error, ECE) for post-EMA epochs, not just lower uncertainty; their predictive intervals will have nominal coverage.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: High awareness subjects show lower ECE (better calibration) for post-EMA epochs compared to pre-EMA epochs; low awareness subjects show no ECE change. If contamination, high awareness shows overconfidence (low uncertainty but high ECE) post-EMA.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Include control (non-stress) EMA prompts to isolate attention effect; measure physiological response to prompt itself (pre-post window).

possible_confounders: Number of observed epochs per subject
Non-stationarity of stress response over study period
control_variables: Minimum epochs per subject (e.g., >50 stress + >50 non-stress)
Compare flat vs. hierarchical versions of same classifier family
Time-in-study as covariate or random slope
boring_rival_explanations: Miscalibration due to small sample size per subject (estimation error)
Non-stationarity: stress response dynamics change over time (habituation, sensitization)
Feature drift: sensor calibration or physiology changes over weeks
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If small sample size causes miscalibration, flat model calibration error will decrease monotonically with increasing epochs per subject for high-variability subjects, eventually achieving nominal coverage.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: With increasing epochs per subject (via subsampling analysis), flat model prediction interval coverage for high-variability subjects remains below nominal (e.g., <90% for 95% intervals) even at large N, while hierarchical model achieves nominal coverage at moderate N; flat model never fully corrects anti-conservatism.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Requires multilevel modeling framework (Bayesian or frequentist); use cross-validation with subject-level folds; test random intercepts, slopes, and AR1 structures.
